# Building the matrix, step by step {#sec-numerical-scheme}

@sec-point-source derives *what* is solved. This chapter is about *how*, at
the level of individual matrix entries, and is meant to be read with an
editor open: everything in it can be rebuilt from scratch in about twenty
lines of NumPy, and every number printed below can be reproduced.

The goal is a working understanding of four things that recur far beyond
this particular code: projecting an integro-differential operator onto an
orthonormal basis; recognising when the resulting matrix is tridiagonal and
why; closing an infinite system *exactly* rather than truncating it; and
splitting one linear system into a sequence that separates physically
distinct contributions. @sec-finite-system states the same results compactly,
as a specification to check an implementation against.

## What is being discretized {#sec-scheme-target}

Everything starts from the one equation established in @sec-adjoint. At a
fixed spatial wavenumber $\mathbf k$ and a fixed frequency $\omega$,

$$
(D-V)h=1,\qquad
D(\mathbf s)=d_0+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf s,\qquad
d_0=\mu_t-i\omega/v .
$$ {#eq-scheme-master}

Three reminders about what the symbols mean, because every later step
depends on reading them correctly.

$h$ is a *function on the unit sphere*, not a number and not a field in
space: $h(\mathbf s)$ for every direction $\mathbf s$. Discretizing means
replacing that function by finitely many numbers.

The right-hand side is the constant function $1$, not a delta function. That
is the whole payoff of reciprocity: the emitted photon direction
$\mathbf s_0$ is absent from @eq-scheme-master and returns only at the end,
when the solved $h$ is *evaluated* at $\mathbf s_0$ to give
$\tilde K(\mathbf k,\omega;\mathbf s_0)$.

$D$ multiplies pointwise — it is a number at each $\mathbf s$, not a
derivative — while $V$ integrates over the sphere. A pointwise multiplier is
trivial in *angle* space and dense in any spectral basis; an integral
operator is the reverse. The basis chosen below is the one that makes the
second one diagonal, and the price is paid in the first.

## Step 1: choose the polar axis along $\mathbf k$ {#sec-scheme-axis}

$\mathbf k$ is fixed while this system is solved, so its direction is
available as a coordinate axis, and nothing forces the same axis to be used
at a different $\mathbf k$. Taking $\widehat{\mathbf k}$ as the polar axis
and writing $\mu=\widehat{\mathbf k}\cdot\mathbf s$,

$$
D=d_0+ik\mu ,\qquad k=|\mathbf k| .
$$

$D$ now depends on one variable instead of two. Both $D$ and the right-hand
side $1$ are unchanged by rotations about the axis, and $V$ is invariant
under *all* rotations, so no azimuthal structure can be generated: the
solution depends on $\mu$ alone. In spherical-harmonic language only $m=0$
is populated, and the problem is one-dimensional.

This step is free, and it is the reason the method costs what it does. It
survives an arbitrary source direction, because $\mathbf s_0$ is not in the
equation (@sec-method-choice). It does *not* survive a directional detector,
whose acceptance is axisymmetric about the module axis instead
(@sec-om-acceptance).

## Step 2: choose the basis {#sec-scheme-basis}

Use Legendre polynomials normalized to unity on $[-1,1]$,

$$
p_\ell(\mu)=\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{2}}\,P_\ell(\mu),
\qquad
\int_{-1}^{1}p_\ell(\mu)\,p_j(\mu)\,\mathrm d\mu=\delta_{\ell j},
$$ {#eq-scheme-basis}

and expand the unknown,
$h(\mu)=\sum_{j\ge0}h_j\,p_j(\mu)$, with $h_j=\int_{-1}^1p_jh\,\mathrm d\mu$.

Two conventions here cause more implementation bugs than anything else in
the chapter, so they are worth stating flatly. First, $p_\ell$ is
orthonormal, $P_\ell$ is not; mixing them misplaces factors of
$\sqrt{(2\ell+1)/2}$ that are easy to hide and hard to find. Second, this
$p_\ell$ is a *basis function* and has nothing to do with the phase function
$p(\cos\Theta)$, which is an unrelated use of the same letter inherited from
the transport literature.

Orthonormality is what makes projection trivial: multiplying by $p_\ell$ and
integrating extracts $h_\ell$ with no metric factor and no matrix inversion.

## Step 3: project, one row at a time {#sec-scheme-rows}

A matrix row is the equation tested against one basis function. Multiply
@eq-scheme-master by $p_\ell(\mu)$ and integrate over $\mu\in[-1,1]$, term
by term.

**The $d_0$ term.** $d_0$ is a constant, so
$\int p_\ell\,d_0\,h\,\mathrm d\mu=d_0h_\ell$. It lands on the diagonal.

**The scattering term.** By @eq-gamma-general, $V$ is diagonal in this basis:
$\int p_\ell\,Vh\,\mathrm d\mu=\gamma_\ell h_\ell$, with
$\gamma_\ell=\mu_s\chi_\ell$, and $\chi_\ell=g^\ell$ for Henyey–Greenstein.
Also on the diagonal.

**The right-hand side.** $\int p_\ell\cdot1\,\mathrm d\mu=\sqrt2\,
\delta_{\ell0}$, since $p_0=1/\sqrt2$ and every higher $p_\ell$ integrates to
zero. Only the first row is forced.

**The streaming term.** This is the only one that couples rows. Multiplying
by $\mu$ is not diagonal, but it is as close as an operator gets:

$$
\mu\,p_\ell=a_\ell\,p_{\ell-1}+a_{\ell+1}\,p_{\ell+1},
\qquad
a_\ell=\frac{\ell}{\sqrt{4\ell^2-1}}\ (\ell\ge1),\quad a_0=0 .
$$ {#eq-scheme-recursion}

This is the standard three-term recursion for Legendre polynomials, rewritten
in the orthonormal basis. Because $\mu p_\ell$ contains *only* the neighbours
$\ell\pm1$, the streaming term produces exactly two off-diagonal entries.
That, and nothing else, is where the tridiagonal structure comes from.

Writing the three rows out explicitly makes the pattern visible. For
$\ell=0$, using $a_0=0$ and $\gamma_0=\mu_s$ so that $d_0-\gamma_0=
\mu_a-i\omega/v$:

$$
(\mu_a-i\omega/v)\,h_0+\frac{ik}{\sqrt3}\,h_1=\sqrt2 .
$$

The disappearance of $\mu_s$ from this row is not an accident — it is photon
number conservation (@sec-number-conservation): scattering moves photons
between directions and cannot remove them from the $\ell=0$ moment. For
$\ell=1$ and $\ell=2$ the right-hand side is zero:

$$
\frac{ik}{\sqrt3}h_0+(d_0-\gamma_1)h_1+\frac{2ik}{\sqrt{15}}h_2=0,
\qquad
\frac{2ik}{\sqrt{15}}h_1+(d_0-\gamma_2)h_2+\frac{3ik}{\sqrt{35}}h_3=0 .
$$

The general row is

$$
\boxed{\;
ik\,a_\ell\,h_{\ell-1}
+(d_0-\gamma_\ell)\,h_\ell
+ik\,a_{\ell+1}\,h_{\ell+1}
=\sqrt2\,\delta_{\ell0}\; }
$$ {#eq-scheme-row}

and the reason it cannot simply be stopped is already visible above: row 2
contains $h_3$. Every row reaches one degree higher than itself.

## Step 4: the infinite tail, and why truncating it is the wrong fix {#sec-scheme-tail}

@eq-scheme-row is an infinite system. The obvious response — keep degrees
$0\ldots L$ and declare $h_{L+1}=0$ — is a modelling choice disguised as a
numerical one, and an expensive one.

The exact alternative costs one extra number. Above $L$ the scattering
coefficients vanish, $\gamma_\ell=0$ for $\ell>L$, and the right-hand side
vanishes too, so every coefficient above $L$ belongs to *free* transport.
The free problem has a known solution: the moments of $1/(d_0+ik\mu)$,

$$
b_\ell=\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{p_\ell(\mu)}{d_0+ik\mu}\,\mathrm d\mu ,
$$ {#eq-scheme-free-moments}

which satisfy the same homogeneous recursion. Of the two solutions of that
recursion, only the decaying one is physical, so the tail of $h$ must be
proportional to the tail of $b$, and in particular

$$
h_{L+1}=r_L\,h_L ,\qquad r_L=\frac{b_{L+1}}{b_L} .
$$ {#eq-scheme-ratio}

Substituting this single relation into row $L$ eliminates $h_{L+1}$ and with
it the entire infinite remainder. Only the last diagonal entry changes:

$$
\boxed{\;
M_{\ell\ell}=d_0-\gamma_\ell\quad(\ell<L),
\qquad
M_{LL}=d_0-\gamma_L+ik\,a_{L+1}\,r_L,
\;}
$$
$$
M_{\ell,\ell-1}=ik\,a_\ell,
\qquad
M_{\ell,\ell+1}=ik\,a_{\ell+1},
\qquad \ell=0,\dots,L .
$$

Every other entry is zero. The matrix is
$(L+1)\times(L+1)$ — one row per retained degree, no more — and it is
complex symmetric, not Hermitian.

How much this matters is a number, not an opinion. For the medium of
`examples/point-green.toml` at $k=0.2\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\omega=0$, comparing
the exact closure against imposing $h_{L+1}=0$ at the same $L$:

| $L$ | exact tail, $h^{(\ge2)}_0$ | truncated, $h^{(\ge2)}_0$ | relative difference |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 3  | $+2.23509176\times10^{-1}$ | $-1.83529526\times10^{-1}$ | $1.8$ |
| 8  | $+2.70399606\times10^{-1}$ | $+2.80471983\times10^{-1}$ | $3.7\times10^{-2}$ |
| 16 | $+2.70251689\times10^{-1}$ | $+2.70262058\times10^{-1}$ | $3.8\times10^{-5}$ |
| 32 | $+2.70251680\times10^{-1}$ | $+2.70251680\times10^{-1}$ | $3.4\times10^{-11}$ |

At $L=3$ truncation does not merely lose accuracy, it returns the wrong
sign. The two agree only once $L$ is large enough that the tail is
negligible anyway — which is exactly the regime the closure exists to avoid
having to reach.

A detail worth internalizing: the ratio @eq-scheme-ratio is *not* computed by
dividing two computed moments. Both $b_{L+1}$ and $b_L$ underflow for large
$L$, and their quotient is then $0/0$. The ratio is computed directly by its
own backward recursion, described in @sec-matrix's collapsed derivation; the
moments themselves are recovered afterwards from the ratios.

## Step 5: why two systems instead of one {#sec-scheme-orders}

@eq-scheme-master could be solved once. The code instead splits
$h=h^{(0)}+h^{(1)}+h^{(\ge2)}$ and solves twice. The reason is that the
three pieces have completely different behaviour in space and time — a
delta, a near-singular front, and a smooth remainder (@sec-histogram-binning)
— and recovering them by subtracting nearly equal totals would destroy the
small one.

Splitting is exact. Expanding $(D-V)h=1$ by collision order,

$$
Dh^{(0)}=1,\qquad
Dh^{(1)}=Vh^{(0)},\qquad
(D-V)h^{(\ge2)}=Vh^{(1)} ,
$$

so that $h^{(0)}=b$ is already known in closed form from
@eq-scheme-free-moments, and the remaining two systems share the matrices
already assembled. With $\Gamma=\operatorname{diag}(\gamma_0,\dots,\gamma_L)$
and $M_{\text{free}}$ denoting the same matrix with every $\gamma_\ell$ set
to zero *but the free-tail term retained*:

$$
\boxed{\;M_{\text{free}}\,\mathbf h^{(1)}=\Gamma\,\mathbf b,
\qquad
M\,\mathbf h^{(\ge2)}=\Gamma\,\mathbf h^{(1)}\; }
$$ {#eq-scheme-two-systems}

The last system sums **all** collision orders from two upward; nothing is
truncated in collision number. $L$ truncates the angular *rank* of the
scattering operator, which is a different statement (@sec-orders).

Neither right-hand side has support above $L$ — each is $\Gamma$ times
something — so the same tail closure is valid for both.

## Step 6: assemble it, with numbers {#sec-scheme-worked}

The following uses the open synthetic parameters of
`examples/point-green.toml` — $\mu_a=0.04$, $\mu_s=0.05$, $g=0.7$ — with
$L=3$, $k=0.2\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\omega=0$, so $d_0=\mu_t=0.09$. A $4\times4$
system is small enough to print in full and large enough to show every
structural feature.

```python
import numpy as np
from lighthit.angular import free_moments_and_tail, solve_tail_system
from lighthit.medium import Medium

med = Medium(0.04, 0.05, 0.7, 1.35, 450.0, "synthetic-example-not-Baikal")
L, k, omega = 3, 0.2, 0.0
d0 = med.extinction_per_m - 1j * omega / med.speed_m_per_ns

ell = np.arange(1, L + 2)
a = ell / np.sqrt(4 * ell**2 - 1)                    # streaming couplings
gamma = med.scattering_per_m * med.g ** np.arange(L + 1)   # scattering
b, tail = free_moments_and_tail([k], d0, L)          # free moments and r_L
b, r_L = b[0], tail[0]

M = (np.diag(d0 - gamma)
     + np.diag(1j * k * a[:-1], 1)
     + np.diag(1j * k * a[:-1], -1))
M_free = (np.diag(np.full(L + 1, d0))
          + np.diag(1j * k * a[:-1], 1)
          + np.diag(1j * k * a[:-1], -1))
M[-1, -1] += 1j * k * a[-1] * r_L                    # the exact tail closure
M_free[-1, -1] += 1j * k * a[-1] * r_L

h1 = np.linalg.solve(M_free, gamma * b)
h2 = np.linalg.solve(M, gamma * h1)
```

The intermediate quantities are

$$
a_\ell=(0.577350,\;0.516398,\;0.507093,\;0.503953),\qquad
\gamma_\ell=(0.05,\;0.035,\;0.0245,\;0.01715),
$$
$$
b_\ell=(8.117179,\;-5.920734\,i,\;-3.915828,\;+2.554428\,i),
\qquad
r_L=-0.649567\,i ,
$$

and the assembled matrix is

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}
0.04 & 0.11547\,i & 0 & 0\\
0.11547\,i & 0.055 & 0.10328\,i & 0\\
0 & 0.10328\,i & 0.0655 & 0.101419\,i\\
0 & 0 & 0.101419\,i & 0.13832
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Everything about this matrix can be read off the derivation. The diagonal is
$d_0-\gamma_\ell=0.09-(0.05,0.035,0.0245,0.01715)$, and the first entry is
$0.04=\mu_a$ exactly, as @sec-scheme-rows requires. The off-diagonals are
$ik\,a_\ell=0.2i\times(0.577350,0.516398,0.507093)$, purely imaginary and
symmetric. The last diagonal entry is *not* $0.09-0.01715=0.07285$: it
carries the tail term $ik\,a_4r_L=0.2i\times0.503953\times(-0.649567i)=
+0.065473$, giving $0.13832$. That single real addition is the entire
infinite tail.

Solving the two systems gives

$$
\mathbf h^{(1)}=(1.648458,\;-2.229996\,i,\;-1.906220,\;+1.525273\,i),
$$
$$
\mathbf h^{(\ge2)}=(0.223509,\;-0.636377\,i,\;-0.666712,\;+0.677959\,i).
$$

The alternation between real and imaginary entries is a consequence of
$\omega=0$, where $d_0$ is real and every off-diagonal is purely imaginary;
it disappears at nonzero frequency and is a useful smoke test at $\omega=0$.

## Step 7: verify the implementation {#sec-scheme-verify}

An implementation that runs is not an implementation that is right. These
five checks are independent of each other and catch different errors; all
five are in the shipped test suite.

**Reproduce the library.** `solve_tail_system` should return the same
vectors as the dense `np.linalg.solve` above. Measured agreement for the
worked example: $1.1\times10^{-15}$ for $\mathbf h^{(1)}$ and
$4.7\times10^{-16}$ for $\mathbf h^{(\ge2)}$. This catches nothing about the
physics and everything about indexing.

**Re-sum the split.** The three pieces must add up to the solution of the
unsplit system, $M(\mathbf b+\mathbf h^{(1)}+\mathbf h^{(\ge2)})=
\sqrt2\,\mathbf e_0$. Measured: $1.8\times10^{-15}$. This catches a wrong
right-hand side in @eq-scheme-two-systems.

**Compare against a different algorithm.** `dense_finite_rank_reference`
solves the same problem by direct Gauss quadrature on the sphere and a dense
resolvent, using neither the tridiagonal elimination nor the tail recursion.
Measured agreement on the worked example: $4.7\times10^{-13}$. This is the
check that the exact tail closure is right, because the two routes share no
part of that reasoning.

**Move a degree that must not matter.** Raising the output degree $J$ while
holding $L$ fixed must not move the low-degree coefficients at all: $J$ is a
reporting length, not part of the linear algebra (@sec-matrix). A test moves
$J$ from 20 to 90 at $L=12$.

**Check a closed form.** At $g=0$ the whole series sums analytically
(@sec-checks), and at $k=0$ the monopole is $1/(\mu_a-i\omega/v)$ for any
$g$ — photon-number conservation again, and the single most useful one-line
check when something is wrong, because it is independent of every angular
detail.

## Common mistakes {#sec-scheme-mistakes}

The failures below are the ones that actually occur, in rough order of how
long they take to find.

*Unnormalized Legendre polynomials.* Using $P_\ell$ with the $a_\ell$ of
@eq-scheme-recursion, or vice versa. The result stays plausible and is wrong
by degree-dependent factors; the $g=0$ closed form catches it at once.

*Dividing the free moments.* Computing $r_L=b_{L+1}/b_L$ from separately
computed moments. Correct for small $L$, $0/0$ for large $L$
(@sec-matrix).

*Forward recursion everywhere.* The free moments are the decaying solution of
their recursion, so forward recursion amplifies rounding error into the
growing solution. This is not a stability nuisance to be dampened, it is a
wrong answer that looks smooth.

*Confusing $L$ with the number of collisions.* $L$ truncates the angular rank
of $V$. The $\ge2$ system sums every collision order (@sec-orders).

*Confusing $J$ with $L$.* $J$ controls only the spatial inversion, and must
track $k_{\max}r$ (@sec-spatial); $L$ controls the scattering operator. Tying
them together produces convergence studies that appear to fail for the wrong
reason, as @sec-bgvd-water documents from experience.

*Assuming diagonality is a Henyey–Greenstein privilege.* It follows from the
kernel depending on $\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf s'$ alone (@eq-gamma-general). A
tabulated phase function changes the numbers $\chi_\ell$, not the structure.

## What the scheme costs {#sec-performance}

The cost is dominated by neither the matrix solve nor the spatial inversion.
Profiling the configuration of `examples/point-green.toml` — $L=32$, $J=160$,
1200 nodes in $k$, 241 frequencies, one observation point — the tridiagonal
sweeps take about $0.4\,\mathrm s$ of a $6.6\,\mathrm s$ solve, while
`_free_moments_and_ratios` takes about $4.5\,\mathrm s$: the free-tail
recursion of @sec-scheme-tail, not the linear algebra it feeds.

That recursion is a scalar three-term sweep, so its cost is the number of
sweeps, and the number of sweeps is set by the Miller start depth
$N+1+\max(32,\lceil28/\eta\rceil)$ of @sec-matrix's callout. Applying one
batch-wide depth charges every node the margin of the slowest-decaying node
in the batch, which by @eq-eta sits at the forward/backward threshold and
needs roughly $9.3N$ extra sweeps. Giving each node its own depth changes no
constant, no tolerance and no result — the outputs are bit-identical — and
removes that excess:

| configuration | batch-wide depth | per-node depth | ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $L=32$, $J=160$, $\omega=0$ | $0.038\,\mathrm s$ | $0.024\,\mathrm s$ | $1.6$ |
| $L=96$, $J=450$, $\omega=0$ | $0.470\,\mathrm s$ | $0.181\,\mathrm s$ | $2.6$ |
| $J=1200$, $\omega=0.6$ | $0.827\,\mathrm s$ | $0.280\,\mathrm s$ | $3.0$ |

End to end the gain is smaller, because the recursion is only one part of a
solve and because at high frequency the batch-wide depth was already close to
the per-node one. Median of three repeats, whole-solve wall time, outputs
bit-identical in every case:

| configuration | batch-wide | per-node | ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $L=32$, $J=160$, 241 frequencies | $10.29\,\mathrm s$ | $8.79\,\mathrm s$ | $1.17$ |
| $L=96$, $J=450$, 41 frequencies | $7.75\,\mathrm s$ | $7.33\,\mathrm s$ | $1.06$ |
| $L=64$, $J=1255$, 5 frequencies | $2.83\,\mathrm s$ | $2.77\,\mathrm s$ | $1.02$ |

The pattern is worth reading rather than averaging: the change pays where
many frequencies are swept, which is the case the spectrum needs, and barely
registers where only a handful are, which is the case a charge-only cache
build needs. It is a real but small effect on its own.

The remaining cost is dominated by *dispatch*, not arithmetic: the recursion
performs one short vector operation per degree, and the loop runs to the
deepest start in the batch. Two routes shorten it, and both have been
measured rather than assumed. Compiling the sweep removes the per-iteration
overhead; the optional Numba backend of `docs/ACCELERATION.md` is that route.
Batching the *frequencies* removes the iterations themselves — the recursion
has identical structure at every $\omega$, so stacking frequencies into the
node axis replaces 241 loops by one, at the cost of holding more
coefficients at once. Measured on the example configuration, in chunks of 32
frequencies, with bit-identical output: $10.6\,\mathrm s\to5.4\,\mathrm s$
for the recursion, a further factor of about $2$. Chunk size matters — 16 and
64 both performed worse than 32 on the test machine — because the working set
has to stay in cache.

Neither route touches $L$, $J$, the quadratures or the constants $3$, $32$
and $28$ that set the recursion's accuracy. Those are the things not to
trade for speed: @sec-discretizations lists what each of them controls.
